one_liner: Header-only drop-in std::shuffle replacement that batches multiple Fisher-Yates draws from one 64-bit random word.
what_it_does: Single-header C++ library providing batched_random::shuffle, a template function matching std::shuffle's signature (first, last, generator) for Fisher-Yates shuffling a range in place. It requires a 64-bit-output URBG (result_type uint64_t, min()==0, max()==UINT64_MAX, e.g. std::mt19937_64) enforced at compile time via static_assert. The API is a drop-in replacement for std::shuffle when that requirement is met; no other configuration is exposed.
how_it_is_fast: Instead of drawing one bounded random value per swap like std::shuffle, it extracts up to 6 bounded Fisher-Yates indices from a single 64-bit random word using 128-bit multiply-shift (Lemire's nearly-divisionless bounded-integer method, from Brackett-Rozinsky & Lemire, arXiv:2408.06213), amortizing each call to the underlying generator across multiple index draws. Batch size (2 through 6) is chosen based on how many elements remain, with rejection resampling on detected bias to keep the shuffle unbiased.
when_to_use: Shuffling std::vector/array of trivially swappable elements with std::mt19937_64 (or any URBG with 64-bit output, min()==0, max()==UINT64_MAX).
Running on libc++ (Apple/LLVM, e.g. macOS/iOS) where std::shuffle's bounded distribution is division-heavy -- biggest measured win (~4.8-5.2x).
Throughput-sensitive shuffling (Monte Carlo simulations, dataset shuffling, deck/card simulations) where shuffle time is a measurable share of runtime.
Header-only vendoring is acceptable -- single file, C++20 toolchain, no build-system integration beyond adding the header.
Array size up to roughly 1 billion elements (technique requires the product of two ranges to fit in 64 bits, per the author).
when_not_to_use: RNG is 32-bit (std::mt19937, std::minstd_rand, etc.) -- fails to compile: static_assert requires result_type==uint64_t.
Already on libstdc++/GCC -- measured gain shrinks to ~30%, may not justify the extra header dependency.
Need a generic std::shuffle drop-in that works with arbitrary/non-standard URBGs without modification.
Project is capped at C++17 or lacks 128-bit multiply support (no __uint128_t on GCC/Clang, no <__msvc_int128.hpp> on MSVC) -- CMakeLists.txt requires C++20.
Tiny project (13 stars, zero issues filed) -- no track record of edge-case bug reports; read the ~120-line header yourself before trusting it in production.

integration.dependencies: none (standard library only: <iterator>, <concepts>, <type_traits>, <limits>; MSVC build also pulls <__msvc_int128.hpp>)
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20); needs __uint128_t (GCC/Clang) or MSVC's _Unsigned128 for 128-bit multiply
integration.platforms: x86-64, aarch64 (anywhere __uint128_t or MSVC's __msvc_int128.hpp is available); CI covers Ubuntu and Windows (VS2022), blog benchmarks ran on Apple M2; no 32-bit platform support documented
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the function holds no global state beyond the passed-in generator reference, so it matches std::shuffle's usual rule: safe only if each thread uses its own generator instance
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial -- explain: same call signature (first, last, generator) as std::shuffle, but only compiles when the generator's result_type is uint64_t with min()==0 and max()==UINT64_MAX (e.g. std::mt19937_64); std::mt19937 and other 32-bit URBGs are rejected at compile time

gotchas: static_assert enforces result_type==uint64_t, min()==0, max()==UINT64_MAX at compile time -- passing std::mt19937 (32-bit) is a compile error, not a runtime one.
Requires 128-bit multiplication (__uint128_t on GCC/Clang, std::_Unsigned128 via <__msvc_int128.hpp> on MSVC) -- a compiler/platform requirement beyond just C++20.

The blog's headline numbers (4.8-5.2x on libc++, ~1.3x on libstdc++) were measured against batched_random::shuffle_2 in a 2024 prototype header, the direct predecessor of this repo; this repo's current batched_random::shuffle uses the same technique (multi-index batches from one 64-bit word) but was not itself the subject of those published numbers.
The repo's own benchmarks/benchmark.cpp runs the identical std::shuffle vs batched_random::shuffle comparison but publishes no results in the repo -- you must build and run it yourself.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Siblings (PCG, Random123, wjakob/pcg32, xoshiro_cpp, biski64, AESRand, nanobench::Rng) replace the RNG itself; cpp_batched_random keeps whatever 64-bit URBG you already use (even std::mt19937_64) and instead speeds up the Fisher-Yates shuffle built on top of it. Pick this when you must keep std::mt19937_64 for reproducibility or statistical-quality reasons but still want faster shuffling, or stack it on top of a sibling 64-bit generator for compounding gains.
verified_claims_summary: Lemire's 2024-08-17 blog post shuffled std::vector<uint64_t> with std::mt19937_64, comparing std::shuffle to the predecessor batched_random::shuffle_2. On an Apple M2 (Apple/LLVM 15, libc++): 12.4 vs 2.4 ns/element at 10,000 elements and 12.0 vs 2.5 ns/element at 1,000,000 elements (~4.8-5.2x; author says 'four to five times faster'). On Linux with an unspecified Intel CPU (GCC 12, libstdc++): 2.2 vs 1.7 ns/element at 10,000 and 3.5 vs 2.7 ns/element at 1,000,000 (~1.3x; author says 'about 30% faster'). I re-fetched the blog page this session and confirmed these numbers match exactly.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-02-28), dual MIT / Apache-2.0-with-LLVM-exception licensed, single ~120-line header with zero open issues and only 13 stars -- small enough to read in full and vendor directly.
